1.2.2 t ypology
Like other South Asian Languages (SALs), Gaddi is a verb-final or a 
subject–object–verb (SOV) word-order language. In the unmarked word 
order, the indirect object precedes the direct object, and the auxiliary 
verb follows the main verb. The complement of verbs and postpositions 
occurs to their left. Like other Indo-Aryan languages, Gaddi lacks bound 
comparative and superlative morphemes. Time adverbials precede place 
adverbials in Gaddi.
Some of the characteristic features of SALs include the use of 
compound verbs (Chatterji 1926; Masica 1976), the presence of conjunct 
verbs, reduplication, and conjunctive participles. Gaddi is no exception. 
Like other Indo-Aryan languages, Gaddi permits pro-drop, which means 
the pronunciation of noun phrases is optional in discourse. It also 
exhibits relatively free word order. As in other Indo-Aryan languages, 
Gaddi has non-nominative subjects. Its relative clauses have co-relatives 
in them. The language only has nominal anaphors, and no verbal ones.
1.2.3 Vitality
While the third edition of the UNESCO’s Atlas of World’s Languages 
in Danger, which refers to the language as ‘Bharmauri’, notes that it 
has a risk factor of being ‘definitely endangered’, our fieldwork did 
not reveal major language loss and endangerment. The language is 
being transferred across generations and, further, it is now used in 
the elementary classroom. However, detailed sociolinguistic profiling 
(Sharma 2016) did reveal that there is an attrition of native-stock 
vocabulary, like kinship terms. Hindi-Urdu, a major language, is found to 
have encroached on the vocabulary of Gaddi. Documenting the language 
extensively and equipping it with a script at this stage can prevent it from 
reaching a critical stage of endangerment. These steps can also facilitate 
primary school education in the mother tongue and help build language 
resources for the community.
1.3 Fieldwork
In 2013 and 2015, students from the Centre for Linguistics at Jawaharlal 
Nehru University conducted linguistic fieldwork as part of the Centre’s 
MA linguistics programme. The first round of data collection in each 
year involved having a native Gaddi speaker in the classroom supply 
Gaddi words and sentences. The Morris Swadesh wordlist, as modified 
by Abbi (2001, p. 248), was used to elicit language data. Abbi’s sentence 
list was also used for the same purpose. The second round of fieldwork, 
in both years, was done in Gaddi settlements close to Palampur town 
in Himachal Pradesh – in the villages of Saperu, Banuri, and Kandbari. 
Participants included both men and women, young adults, and the 
elderly. A third round of data collection was done online in February 
2022 to fill the gaps in the data from 2013 and 2015 for the purposes 
of this book.

2.1 Introduction
This chapter analyses the various phonetic and phonemic properties of 
the sound system of Gaddi. These include the phonetic and phonemic 
description of vowels, the syllable structure of the phonemes and 
their consequent combinatorial constraints, the different phonological 
processes undergone by Gaddi phonemes, and the morphophonological 
processes.
2.2 Vowels
‘Vowel’ here refers to the vowel sounds in a language. These typically 
occur as the essential centres of syllables. For example, in English, in 
words like ‘car’ and ‘fan’, the vowel letter is ‘a’. But is the vowel sound 
the same in both words? The answer is no. In the case of ‘car’, the vowel 
sound is /a/, and in the case of ‘fan’, the vowel sound is /æ/. This section 
deals with finding the various vowel sounds in Gaddi.
The vowel inventory of Gaddi was arrived at by collecting minimal 
and near-minimal pairs for all vowels. In phonology, a minimal pair 
is a set of two words that vary by one sound or a single phonological 
element. For example, words like ‘pat’ and ‘pet’ in English differ by a 
single vowel sound such that the meaning of the entire word changes. 
As it is not easy to find perfect minimal pairs in a language, such that 
they are completely identical except for one element, we look for near-
minimal pairs where the pair of words seem mostly identical except for 
the contrastive elements. Our major focus is to find these contrastive 
phonological units or sounds that constitute the phonemic inventory of 
the language.
Gaddi has eight distinctive oral monophthong vowels, three nasal 
vowels, and nine diphthongs. Out of these nine diphthongs, five are oral 
and four are nasal. Gaddi, therefore, belongs to the category of large 
vowel inventory languages.
Vowels in Gaddi can be specified on three dimensions:
• Place
• Nasality
• Length

2.2.2 Nasality
Gaddi has three nasal vowels: /ũ/, /ɑ̃/, and /ɛ̃ /. Their occurrence is not 
contingent on a phonological process such as nasal assimilation, where a 
vowel is positioned adjacent to a nasal consonant and thereby assimilates 
to it by becoming nasalised. These are rather inherently nasal segments. 
All three vowels show length distinction, but the distinction in length 
is not contrastive. 1 The speakers produce both long and short counter -
parts interchangeably. Vowel length distinction in Gaddi is discussed in 
detail in the following section. Examples (6), (7), and (8) show instances 
of the three lexical nasal vowels and their long counterparts.

2.4 Phonotactics

combination of phonemes in a language. The phonotactic constraints 
define the restrictions of the phonemes with respect to (i) their distribu -
tion in word-initial, medial, and final positions and (ii) their occurrence 
with respect to other adjacent segments. The following section describes 
the selectional and combinatorial constraints of consonants and vowels, 
respectively.

Given the phonotactic restrictions that govern the constituent structure 
of the syllable in Gaddi, we can break down the canonical syllable into 
several types – monosyllables, disyllables, and polysyllables. The mono-
syllables are words consisting of only one syllable, disyllabic words 
consist of two syllables, and polysyllables consist of three or more 
syllables.
One of the main ideas behind understanding what constitutes a 
well-formed syllable in a language is its compliance with the sonority 
hierarchy. The idea is that the nucleus of each syllable constitutes a 
sonority peak, while the other segments belonging to the same syllable 
are arranged according to a falling sonority profile from the nucleus 
outwards (Brockhaus-Grand 1999). Put simply, sonority should rise 
from the onset towards the nucleus, reach the sonority peak at the 
nucleus and then fall towards the coda. This is called the Sonority 
Sequencing Principle.
The sonority hierarchy is as follows in its increasing order of 
sonority:
Plosives >> Fricatives >> Nasals >> Laterals >> Flaps >> 
Vowels
It can be clearly seen that the examples in (14) conform to the sonority 
hierarchy. Thus, we understand that these are legitimate syllables in 
Gaddi.

As discussed in the previous section, a syllable is a unit of pronunciation. 
Therefore, it becomes essential for us to study the syllable division in 
Gaddi from a phonological perspective. For example, the word ‘peruse’ 
in English is syllabified as pe/ruse and not per/use. To understand how 
words are divided into different syllables, we need to trace the segments 
that serve as onsets and codas. For the sake of simplicity of description, 
we are going to follow the method adopted by Asher and Kumari (1997) 
to divide word-medial segments:
What is therefore proposed here is that we take consonant classes 
rather than actual segments in the consonant system. Three major 
types of consonants are needed: ‘i’ stops, oral and nasal ‘P’; ‘ii’ 
fricatives ‘F’; and ‘iii’ liquids and glides ‘L’. This makes it possible to 
show that the onset of all syllables has the same structure as that 
allowable for word-initial consonants, and that the coda of any 
syllable has the same structure as the possibilities for word-final 
consonants. (Asher and Kumari 1997, p. 429)
We also consider here the speaker’s intuitions of syllable division. 
These judgements, in addition to the word-initial consonants, may 
give us a clearer picture of the permissible coda and onset consonants, 
respectively.

In every language, syllables tend to maximise their onset or maximise 
their coda. The nuclear material is identified first, followed by the onset 
or coda, depending on which gets maximised in the respective language. 
Given Gaddi’s phonotactic constraints, 4 we can determine whether the 
language is onset maximal or coda maximal.
Let us consider Gaddi to be coda maximal. The next step would be 
to identify the codas and then finally associate the onset to the rhyme. 
However, as seen in the above examples, Gaddi allows a coda consonant 
only if there is a geminate consonant or if the following syllable has a 
complex onset. 
Now, consider Gaddi to be onset maximal. The steps then would be 
to identify the nucleus (see Figure 2.1), then the onset, and then finally 
one would associate the coda (if any), to construct a full syllable. The 
syllables then perfectly comply with the phonotactic constraints of the 
language and are, therefore, well-formed syllables. Thus, we understand 
the constituent structure of Gaddi to follow the Onset Maximisation 
Principle, which is defined as intervocalic consonants being maximally 
assigned to the onsets of syllables in conformity with universal and 
language-specific conditions (Kahn 1980).

Nasal vowels and diphthongs
context_notes:
Nasal vowels are found in many languages, but unlike nasal consonants, 
these are not so common. It is not necessarily the case that if a language 
has nasal consonants, it will have nasal vowels. The most common nasal 
vowel across all languages is the low vowel [ ɑ̃]. The maximum number 
of nasal vowels in a language can be the corresponding number of oral 
vowels in that language, and typically, the number is from three to seven 
(Ferguson 1963). Nasal vowels when in the word-final position and 
when following a non-nasal consonant showcase maximum contrast. 
When nasal vowels are adjacent to a nasal consonant or another nasal 
vowel, there is minimum contrast.
Gaddi has three nasal vowels /ũ/, / ɑ̃/, and /ɛ̃/ and four nasalised 
diphthongs /əũ/, /ɛ̃i/, /iũ/, and /aũ/, as discussed in the earlier sections 
(see Section 2.2.2).
Contextual nasalisation
Vowels assimilate to surrounding nasal consonants in many languages, 
creating nasal vowel allophones. Some languages exhibit a nasalisation 
of segments that are adjacent to phonemic or allophonic nasal vowels. 
This could also be referred to as nasal assimilation. Here, two or more 
segments in a form agree in their value for some phonological features 
or feature classes.

In Gaddi, we see that there is local assimilation that takes place; that 
is, it takes place between adjacent segments. The vowel takes up the 
feature [+nasal] from the following nasal consonant and therefore gets

context_notes:
The spread of nasality from one segment to another is a universal 
phenomenon found across many languages. This is apparent in vowels 
becoming nasalised preceding a nasal consonant. The spread of 
nasality can be regressive or progressive from a nasal consonant to 
a neighbouring vowel, but regressive nasal spread is more common. 
Nasal spreading from a consonant to the neighbouring vowel can 
stop partway through the vowel or can proceed all the way to the next 
syllable unless blocked by another consonant. ‘Consonants differ in 
the amount of resistance they offer to nasal spread: glottal consonants 
(/h/ or /?/) offer least resistance, liquids and semivowels somewhat 
more, and voiced fricatives still more; only rarely does nasality spread 
across voiceless obstruent’ (Ferguson 1975). Let us consider the case of 
Gaddi.

Prenasalised consonants are phonetic sequences of nasals and obstruents. 
Gaddi also displays prenasalisation in some contexts. Perceptually, 
prenasalisation was not evident at first, but after a close auditory and 
acoustic analysis, we could clearly find prenasalisation taking place. 
The effect of prenasalisation is quite interesting in Gaddi. In Gaddi, 
the process of prenasalisation takes place word-initially before voiced 
plosives. Let us look at some examples.

2.9.6 Retroflexion
A retroflex consonant is a coronal consonant where the tongue has a flat, 
concave, or even curled shape and is articulated between the alveolar ridge 
and the hard palate. The four main characteristics of retroflexes (Hamann 
2003) are apicality, posteriority, sublingual cavity, and retraction.
Cross-linguistically, retroflexes are known to be marked because of 
their articulatory complexity and their context-dependent perceptibility. 
Retroflexes occur relatively infrequently cross-linguistically; for instance, 
only 11 per cent of the languages of the world have a retroflex stop. This 
restricted occurrence of the retroflex class can be attributed to their artic-
ulatory complexity as retroflection involves raising and displacement of 
the tongue tip towards the post-alveolar region as compared to apical 
alveolar sounds, which involve only the tongue tip raising.
Gaddi has seven distinctive retroflex sounds, all of which are 
coronal. These are:
[ʈ	ɖ] – retroflex unaspirated plosives
[ʈʰ	ɖʰ] – retroflex aspirated plosives
[ɳ] – retroflex nasal
[ɽ] – retroflex flap
[ɭ] – retroflex lateral approximant
Of these, six are oral [ʈ	ɖ	ʈʰ	ɖʰ	ɽ	ɭ] and one nasal [ɳ]. The sounds /ʈ/ and 
/ʈʰ/ are voiceless and the rest are voiced. Some examples of the retroflex 
sounds of Gaddi can be seen in (33) to (36) as retroflexed plosives,

2.10 Morphophonological processes
Morphophonological processes are borne out of word-margin interac -
tions. Upon the addition of morphemes to a stem, the syllable make-up 
of the edge of the word to which the respective morpheme is added 
gets altered. In such a situation, the word resyllabifies to restore its 
syllable design. Resyllabification can result in a variety of phonolog -
ical phenomena. Since these processes occur due to the interaction of 
multiple morphemes, we will study them all under the umbrella term of 
morphophonology.

3.2 Nouns
Nouns, along with verbs, are universal and a principal part of speech, 
found in all languages (Matthews 2007). They represent a class of lexical 
words that denote concrete entities (like table, cup, man) or abstract ones 
(happiness, grief, enthusiasm). They can change shape or have affixes 
added to them, that is, they can inflect for noun class (grammatical 
gender, for instance), number, and case morphology. Their distribution 
is such that they can be the subject of a clause or the object of a verb or 
postposition. They co-occur with adjectives and can be a constituent in 
a nominal compound verb. They can also modify a noun to form noun–
noun compounds.
Many languages classify their nouns into semantic classes. Gaddi 
nouns are categorised into a single noun class of grammatical gender. 
They classify themselves as either masculine or feminine.
Gaddi nouns inflect for grammatical gender and number, and 
supplete for case morphology. In this section we discuss these three 
properties of Gaddi nouns in some detail. We then move on to discuss 
derived nouns, that is, nouns generated from verbs, adjectives, and other 
nouns. The section ends with a brief discussion on the etymological map 
of Gaddi nouns.
Nouns in Gaddi are assigned a two-way grammatical gender 
feature with two values: masculine (M) or feminine (F). The assignment 
of grammatical gender to the noun is mostly arbitrary, as is evident 
from the examples in (47) and (48). The inflections on the verb and the 
adjective/quantifier modifying the noun depend on the gender of the 
noun. This is discussed at length in the following chapter.

Pronouns are words that are used in place of nouns and noun phrases.

the box that fell off the table). Nominal features like person, number, and 
gender also manifest on pronouns. Further, pronouns may inflect for 
case. In English, the nominative pronoun in (73), for example, is distinct 
from the accusative marked one in (74).

3.4 Verbs
Often referred to as the central player of an utterance, verbs are 
 argument-picking lexical items that tend to denote either some kind of 
state, process, or action. Co-occurring with arguments of the utterance, 
they generally give us a lot of information about tense, aspect, voice, 
mood, event type, and agreement features of the participants involved 
in the utterance. The agreement features are usually person, number, 
gender, and honorificity (PNGH). This is why a study of the fully 
inflected verb is central in understanding the utterance in question.
In Gaddi too, verbs form the core of clauses and play a very 
important role in determining the identity of the action being commu -
nicated. They also mirror key semantic and syntactic characteristics of 
the sentence, along with their lexical interpretation, making it possible 
to decode finer encodings like the number of participants involved, the 
temporal frame of reference, the manner of occurrence, the speaker’s 
perception, and the internal temporal constituency of said action. Along 
with functioning as the main verb, they are found in other capacities, and 
this chapter highlights each of them.
While Chapter 4 shall focus on presenting a comprehensive view 
of inflections and the complete verb morphology, the discussion here 
focusses on presenting an overview of the nature and the semantic 
interpretation of Gaddi verbs. The proposed citation form of the verbs is 
represented with the infinitival form – with the suffix -ɳɑ – as in pəɽɳɑ ‘to 
read’, for instance. 
3.4.1 Verb types
Some verbs in Gaddi only take a subject, that is, they do not take an 
object and are intransitive in nature. These include verbs like kʰɑŋɡɳɑ 
‘to cough’ and roɳɑ ‘to cry’. Those that select a direct object along with 
a subject (transitive verbs) are found in abundance. A few commonly 
used transitive verbs are kʰɑɳɑ ‘to eat’, kɑʈɳɑ ‘to cut’, and likʰɳɑ ‘to 
write’. Ditransitive verbs are verbs that require both a direct and 
an indirect object, along with a subject, for their full meaning to be 
realised. These are verbs such as diɳɑ ‘to give’, and k ʰəridɳɑ ‘to buy’. 
Derived from the intransitive, transitive, and ditransitive verbs are the 
causative forms of verbs. These are verbs which require an additional 
argument or initiator.
According to Masica (1991, p. 318), Abbi (2001), and Kachru 
(1966), most Indo-Aryan languages form causatives either by peri -
phrastic constructions or with the use of suffixes. Typically, an intransi -
tive verb has the potential to be a transitive and then a causative, that is, 
a structure with two and three arguments, respectively. Gaddi makes use 
of suffixes to build the causative. The following examples illustrate this. 
Let us first look at (89), where the verb is intransitive.

3.4.2 Classification of Gaddi verbs
Based on Levin ( 1993) and Levin and Rappaport Hovav (1995), 
Gaddi verbs can be broadly classified into 10 classes, namely, ‘verbs 
of motion’,  ‘verbs of change of state’, ‘verbs of perception’, ‘verbs of 
consumption’, ‘verbs of image impression’, ‘verbs of bodily processes’, 
‘verbs of spatial configuration’, ‘verbs of existence, appearance, and 
disappearance’, ‘verbs of emission’, and ‘verbs of contact/attachment’. 
The motivation for this classification comes from the fact that verbs that 
belong to the same group behave morphologically in a similar fashion; 
   MA joR  woRD  CLASSeS  53
for example, they display the same kind of and number of intransitive, 
transitive, and causative forms. The following discussion of the classifica-
tion highlights this.
Verbs of motion
Those verbs in Gaddi that function as giving the interpretation of causing 
something – externally or naturally – or specify how the motion takes 
place can be placed in this category. These verbs are found to have both 
transitive and causative variants in Gaddi. Some such verbs are: uɖɳɑ 
‘to fly’, tʃəlɳɑ ‘to walk’, ɡʰumɳɑ ‘to turn/roam’, peɳɳɑ ‘to put’, tʃəɭəɳɑ ‘to 
drive’, terɳɑ ‘to swim’, bəɖɳɑ ‘to enter’, tʃukɳɑ ‘to lift’, ɡʰumɳɑ ‘to roam’, 
tʃʰɑdɳɑ ‘to quit’, bəɖəlɳɑ ‘to turn’, bʰədʒɳɑ ‘to transfer’, dəŋɡɳɑ ‘to strike’, 
bəhɳɑ ‘to flow’, kʰəɳɳɑ ‘to dig’, peiɳɑ ‘to fall’, and leɳɑ ‘to take’.
Verbs of change of state
In Gaddi, the set of verbs that describe a change of state or a course 
of development of the entities are placed under this category. These 
could be either caused externally or have an inherent natural course 
of development. These verbs are also found to have both transitive and 
causative variants in Gaddi; kʰilɳɑ/kʰidɳɑ ‘to bloom’, həkɳɑ ‘to dry’, 
dʒəmɳɑ ‘to solidify/freeze’, truʈɳɑ/bʰədʒɳɑ ‘to break’, bənɑɳɑ ‘to make/
cook’, bədəlɳɑ ‘to change’, ɡʰuhɑɖɳɑ/kholɳɑ ‘to open’, uʈʰɳɑ ‘to wake’, 
muskurana ‘to smile’, and ʃərmɑnɑ ‘to be shy’ are a few such verbs.
Verbs of perception
Those verbs that involve the act of perceiving a said object or event or 
state can be categorised in Gaddi as verbs of perception. Verbs in this 
class are transitive and also permit causative and ditransitive variants. 
Some verbs of perception are: sunɳɑ ‘to listen’, dekʰɳɑ/herɳɑ ‘to see’, 
huɳɳɑ ‘to listen’, bəlɳɑ ‘to speak’, dʒɑnaɳɑ ‘to know’, ləɡɳɑ ‘to feel’, tʃəkʰɳɑ 
‘to taste’, tʃɑɳɑ ‘to want’, and tʃuɳɑ ‘to touch’.
Verbs of consumption
Verbs that tend to describe atelic bodily activities like ingestion 
and swallowing can be classified into the category called verbs of 
consumption. These verbs are transitive, and they also have ditransitive 
and causative variants in Gaddi; kʰɑɳɑ ‘to eat’, piɳɑ ‘to drink’, kʰilɑɳɑ ‘to 
feed’, niɡəlɳɑ ‘to swallow’, leɳɑ ‘to have/take’, pəɳɳɑ ‘to put’, and tʃɑɳɑ ‘to 
want’ are a few verbs from this class.
Verbs of image impression
These include verbs like ‘embroider’ and ‘engrave’. They are activities 
and events that involve an action that displays some ‘image’. These 
are transitive in nature, and they have their causative and ditransitive 
variants in the language as well; rəŋɡɳɑ ‘to paint’, pəɽɳɑ ‘to read’, and 
likʰɳɑ ‘to write’ are verbs of image impression.
Verbs of bodily processes
These kinds of verbs describe corporeal processes in Gaddi that are 
mostly internally caused and thus don’t tend to have any transitive or 
causative variants. These are verbs such as tʰukɳɑ ‘to spit’, kʰɑŋɡɳɑ ‘to 
cough’, roɳɑ ‘to cry’, həsɳɑ ‘to laugh’, uʈʰɳɑ ‘to wake’, ʃərmɑnɑ ‘to be shy’, 
muskurana ‘to smile’, dekʰɳɑ/herɳɑ ‘to see’, huɳɳɑ ‘to listen’, dəŋɡɳɑ ‘to 
stink’, bəlɳɑ ‘to speak’, ləɡɳɑ ‘to feel’, tʃəkʰɳɑ ‘to taste’, and tʃɑɳɑ ‘to want’.
Verbs of spatial configuration
Levin and Rappaport Hovav (1995) suggest that verbs of this kind specify 
the position of an entity that ‘bears a particular spatial configuration with 
respect to that position’, that is, either a maintained, an assumed, or a 
simple position. In Gaddi, these verbs have both transitive and causative 
uses; ləʈəkɳɑ ‘to hang’, beʃɳɑ ‘to sit’, and kʰədɳɑ ‘to stand’ are verbs of 
spatial configuration.
Verbs of existence, appearance, and disappearance
Discussing Hindi verbs, Richa (2008) describes this class of verbs as that 
which describe eventualities involving two participants: a theme (that is, 
an entity whose existence is asserted) and a location. Such verbs in Gaddi 
lack transitive and causative variants. Some such verbs are rɛɳɑ ‘to live/
stay’, mərɳɑ ‘to die’, uʈʰɳɑ ‘to wake’, hoɳɑ ‘to be’, bʰuɳɑ ‘to happen’, tʃəlɳɑ 
‘to walk’, and kʰolɳɑ ‘to open’.
Emission verbs
Verbs in Gaddi that represent some kind of emission or release are 
grouped in this category. They tend to mostly be used only as an intransi-
tive. A select few, the ones that can be externally caused, can be used as 
a transitive and causative as well, such as the verb ‘to sing’. Other verbs 
that qualify as emission verbs are roɳɑ ‘to cry’, ɡurrana ‘to roar’, kəɽəkɳɑ 
‘to thunder’, bədʒɳa ‘to ring’, and dəŋɡɳɑ ‘to stink’.
Verbs of contact/attachment
In Gaddi, those verbs that have attained a result-state and describe the 
attained physical location of physical objects are members of the class 
of verbs called verbs of contact/attachment. These are also referred 
to as verbs of accomplishment. The verbs t ʃipakɳɑ ‘to stick’, l əɡɑɳɑ ‘to 
put/attach’, m ɑrɳɑ ‘to beat’, and ləɡɳɑ ‘to feel’ are a few verbs of this 
class.

3.6 Adpositions
Gaddi has two types of adposition markers: noun dependent and noun

nominative, the accusative, the dative, the ergative, the oblique, and

subject-oblique manifest themselves by modifying the suppletive stems 
of simple noun phrases and appear as clitics on complex noun phrases. 
Noun-independent adpositions are the case makers for the ablative, 
the instrumental, and the locative cases. These adposition markers are

3.8 Numerals5
Numerals are that part of speech in a language which describes any 
relationship that can be valued in countable terms. These relationships 
broadly fall under five types: (i) quantity, (ii) sequence/order, (iii) 
proportion, (iv) frequency, and (v) distribution. These relationships are 
expressed by cardinal, ordinal, fractional, multiplicative, and distributive 
5 The data in this section is from Kumari ( 2016, 2021), as well as from her doctoral fieldwork 
 database of Gaddi (personal communication).
numerals, respectively. The remainder of this chapter will describe the 
formation of the numerals in Gaddi.
The numerals in every counting system can be identified as atoms 
and syntagms. While the former are simple underived lexical expressions, 
the latter are derived from the atoms (Greenberg 1978; Winter 1992).
Every counting system has a base. The base is the number of 
unique digits in terms of which all the other numbers are represented. 
Typologically, different languages can have different bases for their 
counting systems. Most modern-day languages use a decimal base system, 
using the number 10 as the base. But there still exist a few languages that 
use other numeral bases for their counting system. Languages in the 
Nigerian Middle Belt, such as Janji and Piti, use a duodecimal system, 
where the number 12 is the base. Some other languages, like Basque 
and Santali, use a vigesimal system, with the number 20 as the base. The 
most common bases are quinary (5), decimal (10), vigesimal (20), and a 
combination of vigesimal and decimal (Comrie 1999). Gaddi, like most 
languages, uses a decimal base system.
Syntactically, the cardinals, ordinals, fractionals, and the restrictive 
numerals are adnominals and precede the noun they modify. All numerals 
come under the category of quantifiers since they modify a noun.
3.8.1 Cardinal numerals
Cardinal numerals are number words that stand for the cardinal numbers. 
Cardinal numbers are numbers that are used for counting. For instance, 
if you saw Ravi’s brothers Arvind, Rajesh, Shashi, and Utpal walk into 
the house and Ravi asked you later, ‘How many of my brothers did you 
see coming in?’, the answer would be the numeral ‘Four’. It would be 
incorrect/infelicitous to respond with any of the responses in (122):

Distributive numerals are number words that answer the question ‘how 
many at a time?’ In other words, the verb phrase has a matching function

instances of boarding permitted at a time.

4.2 Noun morphology
4.2.1 Case morphology
Morphological case is an inflectional category of nouns which marks 
their role in relation to other parts of the sentence, including subjects and 
objects (Matthews 2007). However, there are two ways the notion of case 
is defined. One is the formal idea of case ‘as an inflected form of a nominal 
word’ (Malchukov and Spencer 2009, p. 2). The other is the ‘semantic’ 
idea of case as a function of a nominal phase in the clause. Under 
the latter definition, phrases marked with prepositions or postpositions 
(rather than purely inflectional markers) are also considered under case 
relations. Here we consider both notions of case to describe Gaddi’s case 
system. In the languages of the world, suffixation is the most common 
way case is realised (Spencer 2009, p. 186). Gaddi is no exception to this.
The traditionally inflecting languages, such as Latin, provide classic 
examples of inflectional case systems. For example, the word ‘hand’ 
in Latin can be manus (nominative), manum (accusative), manuus 
(genitive), manuii (dative), or manuu (ablative), depending on the case 
in question (Blake 2001). This type of system is opposed to languages 
like Japanese or Hindi-Urdu, where grammatical relations are expressed 
by means of particles like -ko (the Hindi-Urdu accusative) or -no (the 
Japanese genitive), which are actually clitic postpositions that attach to 
the entire noun phrase. Gaddi has a Japanese/Hindi-Urdu-type system of 
case markers. Next, we detail the various morphological cases in Gaddi.1

4.3 Verb morphology
Finite verb forms in the language are built with the verb root as the base. 
All exponents that represent various attributes of the inflected finite 
verb form are attached as suffixes onto the verb root. The maximal verb 
template consists of two suffix positions after the verb root, and there 
were no exponents found to be prefixal. Along with verbs, auxiliaries 
play a very important role in reflecting key details about the verbal 
situation in question.
The inflections found on the verb tend to play a very important 
role in describing information related to the temporal reference of the 
event, its internal constituency, the speaker’s perception about said 
event, and the controller or participants that directly and indirectly 
relate to said activity or event. An examination of these inflections 
presents a fascinating set of properties of the language, a few of which 
resemble typical Indo-Aryan features. The following subsections discuss 
the various verbal inflections found in Gaddi and attempt to highlight 
these features as they arise.
4.3.1 Verb agreement
Most of the affixes in Gaddi are fusional in nature and represent a bundle 
of one or more agreement feature values at the least, along with other 
temporal, aspectual, and modal details. Therefore, it is crucial to begin 
the discussion on verb morphology with agreement in order to fully 
decode the intricacies of the morphology of the verb in a Gaddi utterance.
According to Steele ( 1978, p. 610), agreement is a ‘systematic 
co-variance relation between a semantic or formal property of one 
element and a formal property of another’. If we look at the two sentences 
in English, I sing a song every day and She sings a song every day, we notice 
that with the change in the subject, there is a change in the verb. It is this 
covariance between the subject and the verb that is termed as agreement.
The element that determines agreement is called the ‘controller’ 
and the other element, whose form is determined by agreement, is called 
the ‘target’. In the two English sentences, the subjects I and She would be 
the controllers and the verb sing the target. We generally indicate and 
define the agreement relation with respect to the agreement features 
that are found to be inherent on the controller, which could be conceptu-
alised as contextually being copied onto the target because of agreement. 
In these sentences, first person singular and third person singular would 
be the respective agreement features.
Agreement has been identified as a very important feature of 
the Indo-Aryan language family, but not all these languages show a 
uniform pattern. According to Masica (1991), verbs of various Indo-Aryan 
languages tend to inflect for the features of person, number, and gender for 
various values to varying degrees. Abbi (2001) states that all Indo-Aryan 
languages linearly display agreement, and it is predominantly the Western 
Indo-Aryan languages that show agreement. For example, the finite verbs 
(and the modifiers of the same) in a language like Hindi-Urdu encode 
information about the controller’s gender and number feature values.
Gaddi verbs display both subject–verb and object–verb agreement. 
Therefore, the demand for the specific feature comes from the controller 
of the agreement, which is either the subject or the object. On the 
controller, the features are inherent. On the verb which is the target, 
the features are contextual. The following few examples aim to illustrate 
the same.

4.3.2 Verb inflections
Information on tense, aspect, and mood along with agreement is reflected 
as inflections on the verbs and the auxiliaries of the verb phrase. Tense, 
aspect, mood (TAM), and agreement are four key pieces of information 
derivable from the finite verbs in Gaddi. Finite verbs have a verb stem 
as the base, which in Gaddi is the verb root, that is, the part without the 
infinitival exponent -ɳɑ.
In some cases, the exponent that attaches to the verb root is a 
representative of just the TAM feature, and then another exponent 
signifying agreement attaches to it. But in some cases, only one exponent 
representing both the TAM feature and agreement attaches to the verb 
root. The constructions involving inchoative aspect and progressive 
aspect can be examples of extended exponence, while those involving 
perfective aspect and imperative mood can be considered an instance of 
cumulation.
According to Masica ( 1991, p. 259), most languages of the 
Indo-Aryan language family comply with the following order of verb 
inflections and agreement features: V-ASPECT-(C)-TENSE/MOOD-C 
and GENDER-NUMBER-PERSON. Gaddi does comply with these 
schemas, and the various representations of its finite verb morphology 
can be accounted for using the two templates, as seen in Figure 4.1.

4.3.3 tense
Tense in Gaddi is identified based on the theory presented in Reichenbach 
(1947), where tense is understood as based on the following three terms: 
E (point of event), S (point of speech), and R (point of reference). 
These labels are used in Figures 4.2 to 4.4. It can be interpreted that 
Gaddi morphologically represents past tense, future tense, and the 
perfect, and these are typically marked on the verb. The present tense 
is morphologically unmarked in the language. Masica ( 1991, p. 282) 
discusses that tense functions are signified by auxiliaries in Indo-Aryan 
languages, although many languages use suffixal morphology to mark 
future temporal reference. Both the future tense construction and the 
past tense construction of Gaddi were found to be similar.
Past tense
In terms of Reichenbach (1947), when the point of event (E) precedes 
the point of speech (S), past tense is pictured in the language, as 
in Figure  4.2. Past tense is formed in Gaddi with the addition of an 
auxiliary at the end of the verbal part of the sentence. The auxiliary 
displays agreement for the features of number, gender, and honorificity. 
The values for past tense are: tʰ-u (masculine singular), tʰ-i (feminine 
singular), or tʰi-jɛ (plural/honorific).

the controller. Other modifiers, like ‘very’ and ‘big’, also participate in the

4.3.4 Aspect
To get a better understanding of the internal temporal constituency of 
an event expressed by a verb and the way events relate to time, a study 
of aspect seems most beneficial. Gaddi verbs inflect for the aspects 
imperfective, perfective, progressive, and inchoative and represent these 
various shades of aspect.
Very much like in the other Indo-Aryan languages of the subcon-
tinent, affixal morphology plays a pivotal role in conveying various 
aspectual connotations in Gaddi. Masica ( 1991, p. 269) claims that the 
usage of secondary constructions (or periphrastic constructions) is a 
common feature used to convey aspectual connotations like progressive 
across various Indo-Aryan languages. Gaddi was found to make use of 
this feature as well, to build the progressive and inchoative aspects.
Imperfective aspect
To describe a situation that is to be viewed with interior composition, 
Gaddi speakers make use of the imperfective aspect. In Gaddi, the 
imperfective aspect is formed by attaching the exponent -d to the verb 
root, after which the exponent for the values for agreement -ɑ/-i/-ɛ 
for masculine/feminine/plural or honorific respectively attaches. The 
sentences in (185) and (186) illustrate the use of the imperfective aspect

When attention is on the internal structure of the event and the event is 
in progress at reference time, we have the progressive aspect at work. In 
Gaddi this is expressed by a periphrastic construction. The exponent for 
the perfective, which agrees for Gend, attaches to the main verb.
Either the exponent - u or the exponent - i attaches to the verb root 
for ma or fe agreement, respectively. In the plural too, the agreement 
feature values are either ma or fe. The second entity is an auxiliary verb 
that is always found to be the imperfective form of the verb kərɳɑ; in other 
words, it is the verb root kər-, to which the imperfective exponent - d is 
attached, followed by the exponent for agreement, -ɑ/-i/-ɛ (masculine/ 
feminine/plural or honorific).

The inchoative aspect is used in Gaddi to indicate the beginning of a 
change in state, and like the progressive construction, it is also formed 
as a periphrastic construction. With the main verb, the exponent - ɳ 
attaches, after which attaches the exponent for agreement – singular 
feature (-a) or plural/honorific feature (- ɛ). The second entity is the 
auxiliary verb in the construction, which is always the perfect form of the 
verb ləɡɳɑ, namely, the verb root ləɡ- with the perfect exponent - ur, to 
which the exponent for agreement, -ɑ/-i/-ɛ (masculine/feminine/plural 
or honorific), attaches.
For example, in (195) the controller is the subject ‘she’, which has 
the value feminine singular. So, to form the inchoative, the verb root 
takes the exponent -ɳ followed by the exponent for singular agreement,

attaches, followed by the exponent -i to denote the feminine singular 
feature representation.

4.3.5 Mood
Gaddi employs certain inflections on the verbs or uses certain inflected 
auxiliaries to denote either the degree of commitment of the speaker 
while making a statement, or the degree of possibility involved in the 
occurrence of the event based on the speaker’s judgement. Since these 
are of modal significance, they are discussed in the following sections 
with the goal of highlighting the range of modal connotations available 
in the language.
Like a couple of Modern Indo-Aryan languages, Gaddi has morpho-
logical representations of the indicative mood and the imperative mood. 
Since neighbouring Tibeto-Burman languages like Kinnauri (Chitkuli) 
and Spiti have representations for the epistemic mood, it is speculated 
that the occurrence of morphological representations for the epistemic 
mood in Gaddi is a result of the same areal feature.
Indicative mood
When the situation or event in question that is mentioned in a statement 
is real or factual according to the speaker’s judgement and the speaker 
wants to express the same, he/she makes use of the indicative mood. 
In Gaddi it is reflected using an auxiliary that is placed at the end of the 
sentence. The auxiliary agrees with the feature’s number and honorificity.
For singular agreement, -ɑ attaches to h-, which appears at the end 
of the sentence. For plural or honorific agreement, - in attaches to h-. 
Present tense too is implied using the indicative mood in the language. 
In copular constructions, the auxiliary is obligatory, but in the rest of the 
constructions involving future or present tense, the auxiliary may or may 
not be present. Interestingly, in the future tense, some constructions are 
coupled with the auxiliary for the indicative mood to perhaps give the 
sense of the irrealis (as seen in (198)). In (198) and (199) the controllers 
of verb agreement are, respectively, ‘letter’ and ‘rain’, which attest the 
value singular. Thus, ha manifests as the indicative marker.

5.3.2 Interrogative
Interrogative sentences are used for asking questions. Interrogatives in 
Gaddi can be classified under two categories – polar or yes/no questions 
and wh-questions.
Polar questions
Polar questions or yes/no questions are types of questions that can only 
be answered with a ‘yes’ or ‘no’. Any other content word cannot form a 
right answer to polar questions. Polar questions in Gaddi are formed by 
inserting the question particle kɛ in the clause-initial or -final position, as 
shown in (220)a–b.
2 Main clauses are clauses that can stand independently without bearing any relation, besides coor-

optional information are therefore called adjuncts.

5.4 Subordinate clauses
Here we present three types of subordinate clauses in Gaddi. These 
clauses are embedded inside the main clause. The word order of the 
subordinate clause remains the same as the main clause, namely, SOV.
5.4.1 Relative clauses
Relative clauses are sentences that modify a noun. For example, in a 
sentence such as ‘The boy who came late to the class is my friend’, the 
phrase ‘who came late to the class’ is a relative clause that modifies or 
provides extra information about the noun ‘boy’. In this sentence, ‘who’ 
is a relative pronoun. Gaddi, like many other Indo-Aryan languages, 
uses a relative as well as a correlative pronoun. For example, the relative 
pronoun in (236) is dʒes and the correlative pronoun is so. These 
pronouns connect the clauses ‘the boy who had fever’ and ‘he died’ to 
each other.5

5.6 Information structure
Gaddi uses morphosyntactic strategies to mark sentence information 
structure, which is the packaging of information in a language, 
considering the state of discourse participants: the speaker and the 
addressee. It includes the notions of topic and focus.
5.6.1 t opic
The topic is that entity in a sentence about which the speaker provides 
information or makes a comment. Gaddi marks the topic by placing it in 
the sentence-initial position. In the canonical word order, the subject, 
which is linearly the first element in the sentence, is also the topic. Let us 
look at the following example.

raw_text:
(260) rɑmmɛ       seb     kʰə-u
 Ram.3sg.m.erg apple eat-pfv.ma.sg
 ‘Ram ate an apple.’
context_notes:
In the example above, it is ‘Ram’ who performed the action ‘ate an apple’, 
and thus it is the topic. If the ‘apple’ were the topic, the sentence would be 
as in (261), with the changed order of words in the sentence the marker 
of topicalisation. The topicalised word occupies the word-initial position 
in this word order.

raw_text:
(261) seb  rɑmmɛ        kʰə-u
 apple  Ram.3sg.m.erg eat-pfv.ma.sg
 ‘Ram ate an apple.’
context_notes:

5.6.2 Focus
Focus is an attribute that indicates those entities of the sentence that 
contribute new or contrastive information. Focus also indicates the 
presence of alternatives (to the focussed entity) that are relevant in 
the conversation. In canonical word order, the focussed entity occupies 
the immediate preverbal position. Thus, in (265), ‘apple’ is focussed.

raw_text:
(265) rɑmmɛ       seb     kʰə-u
 Ram.3sg.m.erg apple eat-pfv.ma.sg
 ‘Ram ate an apple.’
context_notes:
Gaddi also uses particles like hi, sirf, and bʰi  to mark focussed elements. 
The particle hi ‘only’ can follow all entities (noun, verb, adverb, adjective, 
preposition, and so on) to ‘emphasise’ the entity in the conversation. 
Example (266) is an example of hi following an adverb.

raw_text:
(266) əũ       əbdʒu-hi   u-ɳ-ɑ  
 1sg.m.nom now-only sleep-inf-sg.m 
 ləɡ-ur-ɑ          hɑ
 begin.happen-prf-sg.m ind
 ‘I will go to sleep now.’ (speaker’s immediate plan)
english_translation: I will go to sleep now.
context_notes:
The hi following the adverb emphasises the meaning of the adverb. The 
speaker intends to say that he will go to sleep immediately after they 
finish this conversation. Apart from emphasis, another use of the particle 
hi is to mark focus-marked nominals, as shown in (267).
Context: Three children, Ram, Sita, and Lala go to the market 
together. They return home, where their mother, worried if the children 
bought their schoolbooks asks, ‘Did you buy your books?’ To this, Sita 
replies with the sentence in (267).

 Ram.3sg.m.erg only book  buy-pfv.fe.sg

context_notes:
Notice that Ram is the focussed entity, but it is not in the preverbal 
position. Another response to the same context is with the use of particle 
sirf ‘only’ before the noun, as shown in (268).

raw_text:
(268) sirf   rɑmme       kətɑb kʰərid-i
 Only  Ram.3sg.m.erg book  buy-pfv.fe.sg
 ‘Only Ram bought books.’
context_notes:
Gaddi has a particle bʰi ‘even’, which gives additive focus to a nominal 
in the discourse. In discourse or conversation, additive focus is used 
to introduce a new entity. This entity must satisfy the predicate of 
a previously mentioned entity. Let us understand this with another 
example.
Context: The context for (267), where Ram, Sita, and Lala go to the 
market, holds and is continued after (267) is uttered. After hearing from 
Sita that only Ram bought books, their mother is furious. Then, Ram 
corrects Sita and tells her the following.

raw_text:
(269) lɑll-ɛ        bʰi    kətɑb kʰərid-i
 Lala.3sg.m-erg too book  buy-pfv.fe.sg
 ‘Lala too bought a book.’
context_notes:
Here, the new entity is the word ‘Lala’. ‘Lala’ satisfies the predicate 
‘bought a book’ of the previously mentioned entity ‘Ram’ (see (267)). 
The focus particle bʰi in (269) marks this addition of the new entity to 
the discourse.
